transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-10-02 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~42m | Attendees: Leah Park (Redwood AE), Marco Silva (Redwood SE), Priya Reddy (AstraHealth, CTO), Daniel Cho (AstraHealth, Lead Eng), Marta Lopez (AstraHealth, PM)

[00:00] Leah Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Leah, I'm the AE on the account. With me is Marco, our systems SE who will drive the demo. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Priya Reddy: Hi Leah, hi Marco, doing well. We've got about 45 minutes, want to make sure we hit streaming and some ops questions.
[00:15] Marco Silva: Great. Quick agenda — show a short live stream generation demo, dig into key params, then talk retries and best practices. We'll leave 10 minutes for security/Qs. Sound good?
[00:27] Daniel Cho: Yes, perfect. We're particularly interested in latency for our triage UI and how to keep costs down.
[00:33] Leah Park: Awesome. I'll hand over to Marco for the walkthrough.
[00:36] Marco Silva: Cool. I'm in the console, I've got a small sandbox app that hits the hosted chat endpoint. I'm going to start a session — we'll do a short prompt, stream the response so you can see tokens arrive. Note: streaming is chunked, you get deltas as the model produces.
[01:02] Marco Silva: (typing) "system: you are an assistant for medical triage prioritization" — then a user message: "Patient with fever 38.5, cough, no shortness of breath, 72 y.o." — send.
[01:20] (streaming output starts) Marco Silva: You can see partial tokens coming in, UI should append rather than replace. If your client reconnects we advise using the conversation_id and last_event_id pattern to resume and avoid duplication.
[01:40] Marta Lopez: Are those partial fragments guaranteed to be in-order? We worry about UI flicker when chunks arrive late.
[01:47] Marco Silva: Generally yes, the stream preserves ordering. On unreliable networks we recommend client-side buffering for small windows (200-500ms) to smooth rendering. For critical UIs you can render token groups rather than single characters.
[02:05] Daniel Cho: What's typical per-token latency we should expect in hosted? sub-200ms per token?
[02:12] Marco Silva: It depends — for small models and short context you can see single-token latencies in the 50–150ms range on our hosted fleet. For larger models or long-history contexts it rises; that's where batching and KV cache help.
[02:29] Priya Reddy: You mentioned KV cache — how does that impact stateful chat?
[02:33] Marco Silva: Good question. We maintain a per-session KV cache so when you request subsequent tokens we avoid recomputing attention over prior tokens in many cases. That reduces CPU/GPU work and latency for follow-ups. Important callout: caching works best when you pin model versions and avoid changing tokenizer or prompt shape mid-session.
[02:55] Leah Park: Quick pause — Marco will now show param effects.
[03:00] Marco Silva: Right — temperature and top_p control randomness. For deterministic summaries we use temperature 0 and top_p 1. Max_tokens controls response length — for streaming you might set a low max_tokens to force concise replies, reduces cost.
[03:20] Marco Silva: I'll change temperature to 0.2 and send same prompt to show difference.
[03:34] (stream shows slightly different phrasing)
[03:52] Marta Lopez: Nice, that looks tighter. Is there a way to enforce a short bullet list in streaming responses?
[03:58] Marco Silva: You can use system messages with explicit instructions and also use stop sequences and max_tokens. Another pattern: request structured output using JSON schema or function-calling so the runtime yields more predictable shapes. Streaming still works for function-style outputs but you may prefer chunked JSON pieces.
[04:20] Daniel Cho: About retries — what should our client do for 429s vs 500s? And idempotency — are calls idempotent?
[04:28] Marco Silva: We recommend exponential backoff for 429s with jitter and longer backoffs for 503/5xx depending on error. For streaming, design idempotency with client-side request ids and de-dup logic. If you replay a request you might get the same content but the model output isn't strictly deterministic. For critical ops, we suggest a try-once-and-fallback pattern: attempt streaming; on fail, fallback to a sync lower-cost model or return cached answer.
[04:58] Priya Reddy: Can Redwood do automatic retries on the server side?
[05:03] Marco Silva: We have server-side retries for transient infra errors in some tiers, but we avoid automatic retries for user-visible model generations since duplication can surface. For hosted customers we expose retry policies in the Console — you can choose aggressive vs conservative.
[05:20] Leah Park: I'm going to show the console panels now — real-time token and cost breakdowns, per-route latency percentiles. Marco, maybe point out the optimize suggestions.
[05:29] Marco Silva: Sure — under Optimize we show batching recommendations based on observed traffic, suggested quantized model variants for cost savings, and per-prompt quality regression flags. For example, if you have many short prompts we recommend lower-latency small models with prefix caching.
[05:45] Marta Lopez: We're concerned about PII. Where does data go and what are retention settings?
[05:50] Marco Silva: Hosted data by default is encrypted at rest and in transit. We support configurable retention, and enterprise customers can opt into stricter retention windows or dedicated capacity where logs are isolated. For compliance we integrate with KMS for customer keying.
[06:10] Daniel Cho: Good. And what's the path for VPC/private? If we need it later, how disruptive is migration?
[06:15] Marco Silva: Migration is supported. Most customers start hosted to validate features then move to Dedicated or Private. We provide a consistent API and rollout tools — you can pin model versions and route traffic to private endpoints with minimal client changes (mostly URL and auth). We ran migrations with a couple hospitals; typical timeline is 4–8 weeks for Private depending on networking.
[06:43] Priya Reddy: That aligns with our risk posture. Any SLA for hosted?
[06:48] Leah Park: SLA tiers exist for Dedicated enterprise. Hosted has uptime guarantees tied to your subscription level; we'll send specifics after the call.
[06:55] Marco Silva: Back to retries — here's a quick table: 429 -> retry with exp backoff starting 200ms + jitter, cap ~2s (for interactive apps). 5xx -> immediate short retry then escalate to fallback model. For streaming partials we recommend checkpointing last_event_id to avoid re-rendering.
[07:18] Daniel Cho: Can you demonstrate a client reconnect flow?
[07:21] Marco Silva: Yep. I'll simulate a dropped connection and resume. (simulating) On resume, client passes conversation_id and last_event_id, server streams the remaining tokens. If server-side cache expired we return a short note and recompute full response — that's why session TTL matters.
[07:46] Marta Lopez: What's a typical session TTL?
[07:50] Marco Silva: Defaults vary by tier; hosted default is 30 minutes for active KV cache, but you can extend for Dedicated. We'll include config knobs in the docs.
[08:03] Priya Reddy: Any guardrails for hallucination in triage context? We need conservative answers.
[08:09] Marco Silva: Two layers — prompt engineering (system prompts, constraints) and model selection. Use smaller deterministic models for factual extraction, then run a second verification step or tool call to your internal rules engine. We also support evaluation suites in Optimize to detect regressions on your prompt set.
[08:30] Daniel Cho: About cost — is per-token charging continuous on streamed tokens?
[08:34] Marco Silva: Yes, tokens emitted are billed. Streaming doesn't change billing semantics; you can reduce cost by lowering max_tokens and using compact prompts. Also caching reduces compute for follow-ups, decreasing per-interaction cost.
[08:50] Leah Park: Quick note: Marco's going to run a short load demo showing parallel requests to demonstrate fallback to cheaper model variant under load.
[08:58] Marco Silva: Running a small load test, 50 concurrent short conversations hitting same model. You'll see autoscaling and fallback where policy routes to a low-cost variant when latency exceeds SLO. (live metrics) You can see 95th p latency spike for the primary but then route rules reduce load within 10s.
[09:28] Priya Reddy: That routing policy looks useful. Are those policies configurable per route?
[09:33] Marco Silva: Yes per-route and per-customer. You can set SLO thresholds, cost ceilings, and fallback model sets.
[09:40] Marta Lopez: Any limits on number of concurrent streaming connections?
[09:44] Marco Silva: Limits are driven by your plan. Hosted tier has soft defaults; Dedicated offers higher concurrency and guaranteed slots. We'll share the exact numbers in the follow-up.
[09:54] Daniel Cho: We're also using WebRTC in our app for low-latency voice + text, any guidance?
[09:59] Marco Silva: WebRTC is used by customers. For voice-gen combined flows we recommend batching at the speech layer and streaming tokens to update UI. We also have examples for client-side playout to handle jitter.
[10:15] Leah Park: Let's shift to a quick Q&A on security specifics before we wrap. Marco, can you cover SSO and audit logs?
[10:21] Marco Silva: Sure — we support SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC, and audit logs that include token-level request traces for enterprise plans. Logs can be pushed to your SIEM via webhook or pulled via API for retention. KMS integration supports CMKs for encryption at rest.
[10:39] Priya Reddy: For SOC2 evidence, do you have a package?
[10:42] Leah Park: Yes, we have SOC2 Type II reports and an enterprise security pack. I'll include the security PO's contact and the pack link after the call.
[10:50] Daniel Cho: Great. A technical nit — how deterministic are function-call responses? We rely on structured JSON back to our orchestrator.
[10:56] Marco Silva: Function calling improves structure but isn't 100% deterministic. You can increase strictness by setting temperature 0 and using schema enforcement. For mission-critical flows pair function outputs with post-validators.
[11:10] Marta Lopez: Any gotchas for migrating from other vendors like Anthropic?
[11:14] Marco Silva: Tokenization differences and prompt tuning are the main items. We help with sample conversion and model-matching during onboarding.
[11:22] Priya Reddy: Ok we're close to time. Can we recap next steps?
[11:26] Leah Park: Sure — we'll send the mentioned cheat-sheets, pricing tiers, and security pack. Marco will attach the retry table and a tiny benchmark script. You (Priya) will confirm pilot scope and traffic dates.
[11:36] Daniel Cho: Sounds good. Also, could we get a small sample request schema for the reconnect flow?
[11:40] Marco Silva: I'll drop that in the follow-up as a gist.
[11:44] Priya Reddy: Thanks — helpful session.
[11:46] Leah Park: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up by Tuesday with the artifacts. Bye!

Notes on transcription: occasional overlaps and minor mishearings. 

End of transcript.
